slides.title: Principled Architectural Design
paragraphs: A desired non-functional profile (i.e., a set of non-functional properties) can be retained by making specific coordinated architectural decisions that restrict individual architectural elements and their interfaces and relationships
**Architectural styles** are abstractions that encapsulate these decisions. They provide guidance towards positioning a system at a specific non-functional trade-off

box.text: As the architect of a (distributed) (information) system, you should be aware of the design trade-offs that are induced by specific choices in order to construct a system with your desired non-functional properties. This is relevant in a (technology) world with projects that exhibit a broad range of non-functional requirements.

slides.title: Case Study 2: Architecture
paragraphs: Architectural elements (windows, walls, arches) are supplied by different stakeholders (masons, carpenters, window builders).
The elements interact through structural mechanics and structural dynamics.
Structural engineers provide coordinated design constraints that comply with the functional and non-functional requirements.
These coordinated constraints might become a recognized architectural style.

slides.title: Case Study 4: The Unix Philosophy
points: Build **modular** programs, use **composition**, separate mechanisms from policy
Write readable, **simple**, **small**, transparent and robust programs
Make data complicated when required, not the program
Build on potential users' expected knowledge; avoid unnecessary output; write programs which fail in a way that is easy to diagnose
Value developer time over machine time; write abstract programs that generate code instead of writing code by hand; prototype software before polishing it
Write **flexible and open** programs; make the program and protocols **extensible**
slides.after: Architecturally: contribution to the toolbox philosophy of Unix

aside.alt: Cover of The Art of UNIX Programming by Eric S. Raymond, and a quote by Doug McIlroy: This is the Unix philosophy: Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.

slides.title: Representational State Transfer
paragraphs: REST is the idealized architectural style of the Web. This does not mean “REST = Web”!
A coordinated set of six architectural constraints: three are explicit in the original Web Architecture, three are explicit in the Modern Web Architecture.
This concrete set of architectural constraints for distributed hypermedia systems is called Representational State Transfer, or REST.
We refer to a system as “REST” if it satisfies all these constraints
**Required reading:** [Fielding's dissertation](https://www.ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/top.htm), at least chapters 4 & 5, recommended everything.

aside.alt: First page of the paper Principled Design of the Modern Web Architecture by Roy T. Fielding and Richard N. Taylor

slides.title: Representational State Transfer
paragraphs: “At the beginning of our efforts within the Internet Engineering Task Force (…) we recognized the need for a model of how the World Wide Web *should* work. This **idealized model of the interactions within an overall Web application**, what we refer to as the Representational State Transfer (REST) architectural style, became the foundation for the **modern Web architecture**, providing the guiding principles by which flaws in the existing architecture could be identified and extensions validated prior to deployment.”
R.T. Fielding and R.N. Taylor, 2002

aside.alt: First page of the paper Principled Design of the Modern Web Architecture by Roy T. Fielding and Richard N. Taylor

slides.title: Representational State Transfer
paragraphs: “Even if it were possible to build a software system that perfectly matches the requirements of its users, those requirements will change over time just as society changes over time. A long-lived system like the Web must be prepared for (…) gradual and fragmented change, where old and new implementations co-exist without preventing the new implementations from making use of their extended capabilities. (…) The introduction of each new goal presents us with a challenge: **how do we introduce a new set of functionality to an architecture that is already widely deployed**, and how do we ensure that its introduction does not adversely impact, or even destroy, the architectural properties that have enabled the Web to succeed? It was this question that motivated our development of the REST architectural style.”
R.T. Fielding and R.N. Taylor, 2002

slides.title: Architectural Constraints on the Modern Web Architecture
paragraphs: Similar to how Lego restricts interfaces and the Bologna Reform restricts study programs, Representational State Transfer (REST) restricts how components may process requests and send responses.

points.text: Six architectural constraints to gain desirable non-functional properties
sub: Three of these were **part of the pre-1994 Web architecture**
Three were added to guide the design of the **modern Web architecture**

points: Together, they continue to make the Web an Internet-scale, open, and long-lived system

slides.title: Components of the Web Architecture
slides.alt: Diagram: an origin client (browser) sends requests through intermediaries (a proxy, a gateway) to origin servers (a web server, a non-web origin server on a Bluetooth device); intermediaries act as clients and servers to forward requests and responses, used for load balancing, caching, bridging and security; components exchange representations of resources, where a resource is anything that might be identified by a URI and a representation is data that encodes information about resource state

groups.heading: Traditional Client/Server Style
points: Render data where it rests
Move **rendered result** to client in **fixed format**
Great simplification of clients!
Server-side scalability problems (large load on server)

groups.heading: Mobile Object Style
points: Encapsulate data with rendering engine; **move both** to the recipient
Great information hiding! Data format does not matter
Limits functionality to what is foreseen in the engine; transmits a lot of data

groups.heading: Prenegotiated Types Style
points: Send raw data to recipient together with metadata that describes it
Remains scalable (load sharing between client and server)
Loses information hiding; requires prenegotiated data types

callout.text: What's meant here? These: [iana.org/assignments/media-types](https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/)

groups.heading: REST Client-Server: Hybrid Style
points: Shared understanding of data types with metadata but **limited to a standardized interface**
Approximation of Mobile Object Style: interaction by **transferring representations** according to an evolving set of dynamically selected standard data types
Gains **separation of concerns** (e.g., UI vs. Data Storage) between **clients** (that send requests) and **servers** (that receive requests and may send responses)

slides.title: Stateless Interactions

callout.text: Client-Server · **Statelessness** · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · Uniform Interface

paragraphs: Each client-server interaction is self-contained and stands alone
State is kept in resources and in the client, but not in the interaction

groups.heading: Resource state is managed on the server
points: It is the same for every client working with the resource
When a client modifies the resource state, other clients see this change as well
The server does not remember the requesting client (no session) nor previous requests (no history)

groups.heading: Application state is managed on the client
points: It is specific for a client and thus has to be maintained by each client
On the Web, this is the purpose of “Cookies”

callout.text: Client-Server · **Statelessness** · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · Uniform Interface

groups.heading: Non-functional benefits
points: **reliability** (easier to recover interaction from partial failures)
**scalability** (takes load off servers, no management of interactions)
**visibility** (easy monitoring)
**load balancing**

groups.heading: Non-functional drawbacks
points: **performance** (repeated transmission of the same data)
**responsiveness** (more complex internal server logic)
**consistency** (less server control over consistent application behavior)

groups.heading: Practically
points: One origin server can easily serve many clients
Intermediaries can reliably interpret requests
Requests can more easily be distributed across different origin servers (load balancing)

slides.alt: A curl request to example.org and its response headers with red annotations: Age and Cache-Control max-age=604800 mean the response is fresh for 604800 seconds and has been cached for 440634 seconds; Etag identifies a version of the resource, used to save bandwidth and to prevent concurrent updates; Expires gives the expiry date, ignored if Cache-Control with max-age is set; X-Cache: HIT means the response was returned from a cache

slides.title: Cacheability

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · **Cacheability** · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · Uniform Interface

paragraphs: Servers must indicate whether their responses may be cached.

groups.heading: Non-functional benefits
points: **performance** (on the network: eliminates interactions)
**responsiveness** (as perceived by the user: eliminates interactions or pre-fetches information)
**scalability** (reduced load on server)

groups.heading: Non-functional drawbacks
points: **reliability** (stale data)

slides.title: Layered System

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · **Layered System** · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · Uniform Interface

paragraphs: Further constrains client-server by restricting visibility to a single component layer. Components are oblivious of whether they communicate with origin servers/clients or with intermediaries

groups.heading: Non-functional benefits
points: **scalability** (scope restriction for components / information hiding)

groups.heading: Non-functional drawbacks
points: **performance** (user-perceived as well as network overhead due to many indirections / marshalling)

slides.title: Code-on-Demand (Optional)

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · **Code-on-Demand (Optional)** · Uniform Interface

paragraphs: Component functionality can be extended by moving and executing code (e.g., scripts).

groups.heading: Non-functional benefits
points: **extensibility** (client behavior can be enriched at run time)

groups.heading: Non-functional drawbacks
points: **maintainability** (through reduced visibility)
**security** (client needs to execute ad-hoc received code)

slides.title: Uniform Interface

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: Component implementations are heterogeneous (different frameworks, data models, formats, etc.). How can they interact in a uniform manner?
Components interact through a general, uniform interface that hides away their implementation details!
Analog: interaction via a shared language (often: EN)
points: Individuals can now interact and understand one another (“interoperability”)

points.text: However, the “uniform interface” is a compromise
sub: Might be a **reduced** interface (i.e., loss of expressivity)
Might be an **inefficient** interface (e.g., for non-native English speakers)

aside.alt: Illustration of a crowd of diverse people of different ages and origins

slides.title: Uniform Interface

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: Components interact through a general, uniform interface that hides away their implementation details! Extension on top of *Layered System* to reduce coupling between components.

points.text: The same (small) set of verbs (i.e., operations) applies to every noun (i.e., resource)
sub: Verbs and their semantics are **universal** and are **not invented per-application**
New **verbs rarely** enter language; new **nouns regularly** do
The same pattern is true for the “English” uniform interface, see [Oxford's New Word Entries](https://www.oed.com/information/updates/september-2024/new-word-entries/)

points.text: For protocols that follow the REST architectural style…
sub: …**noun semantics** are defined by **media types** (e.g., application/json for JSON)
…**verb semantics** are defined in the **protocols** (e.g., in HTTP)

aside.alt: Table of contents of RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, section 9 Methods: common method properties (safe, idempotent, caching) and the method definitions GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE
aside.caption: The methods apply to every resource. The methods have global semantics.

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

defs: retrieves the representation of a resource
identical to GET but server must not send content
request information about communication options of resource
replaces the state of a resource with the one enclosed in the body of the request
(added through RFC 5789) apply specified changes to resource
wildcard method, typically used for creating or updating a resource
slides.after: GET, HEAD: safe, idempotent, cacheable · PUT, DELETE: idempotent · POST: neither safe nor idempotent

aside.alt: Some notes on GET requests: they can be cached, remain in the browser history, can be bookmarked, should never be used with sensitive data, have length restrictions and only request data. Some notes on POST requests: never cached, not in the browser history, cannot be bookmarked, no restrictions on data length
aside.caption: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

groups.heading: Non-functional benefits
points: **evolvability / extensibility / interoperability** (permits independent evolution of components)
**maintainability / visibility** (easier to monitor interactions)
**simplicity**

groups.heading: Non-functional drawbacks
points: **performance** (general uniform interface is not optimized for specific applications)

slides.title: What aspects are “uniform”?

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

slides.lead: **The interface itself:** there is only a small set of general methods (e.g., GET, POST, etc.) that apply to any resource. **The transmitted representations:** their semantics are defined using media types.
slides.alt: A user agent sends HTTP PUT with the application/json body {"on": true} to an intermediary or origin server next to a light bulb and gets 200 Ok. Does this really specify the semantics of the interaction? No… So what now? We could agree on a sub-type to define the intended semantics, e.g. application/bulb+json. On this level, semantics are simply “documented consensus among people”; this consensus is then programmed into a machine. More in 3 weeks

slides.title: REST's 4 Uniform Interface Constraints

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: 1. Resources must have uniform identifiers that are uniquely addressable using a universal syntax
2. There is no direct access to resources. Rather, components exchange representations of resources and manipulate resources via representations.
3. Messages must be self-descriptive. They need to include metadata that describes their meaning.
4. The state of the client-server application is guided by server-provided hyperlinks.

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

points.text: Name everything you want to talk about in your application. Those are resources.
sub: **Products** in an online shop, **customers** that are expected to buy products, **shopping carts** where customers collect products
**Next** links on multi-page submission processes or **paged** results
**Robots** in a laboratory: [api.interactions.ics.unisg.ch/cherrybot](https://api.interactions.ics.unisg.ch/cherrybot/)

points.text: The standard RFC 3986 “URI” defines the term “resource” as anything that might be referred to by a URI.
sub: **Abstract** concepts can also be resources
**Non-network-retrievable** artifacts can also be resources: [github.com/smnmyr#me](https://github.com/smnmyr#me)

points.text: Resources have uniform identifiers that are uniquely addressable using a universal syntax
sub: They should mean the same anywhere (think load balancing, but also intranets or DNS spoofing)

aside.alt: Google's result pages: Gooooooooooogle with page numbers 1 to 10 and a Next link

slides.title: (2/4) Manipulation via Representations

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: Resources are abstract entities and cannot be used per se

groups.heading: Interaction with resources happens via resource representations
points: Clients don't have access to resources but exchange **representations** with servers
It is **communicated** which kind of representation is used: content negotiation establishes a **contract**
Representation formats can be **negotiated between peers**

groups.heading: When you access a Web resource, you see one of its representations
points: Your browser **negotiates** for you! (HTML, locale/language, context attributes)
If a machine accesses a Web resource instead of a person, it will (should!) see a **different representation**

slides.title: (3/4) Self-descriptive Messages

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: A message (e.g., HTTP request, CoAP response) must include metadata that describes its meaning; this includes standard verbs and media types
slides.after: Clients, Servers, and Intermediaries can interpret messages (e.g., to help the Web scale up)

aside.alt: A captured HTTP response in Wireshark with red annotations: HTTP/1.1 200 OK is the response status code (and HTTP version), Content-Type: text/html is the media type of the response, Cache-Control and Expires are cache control metadata, Content-Length is the payload length

slides.title: (4/4) Guidance through Server-Provided Hyperlinks

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

paragraphs: In REST, servers give local guidance to clients through hyperlinks. Hyperlinks are possible state transitions of the client/server application

groups.heading: Clients don't “call services”, they “navigate application states”
points: In REST, clients **discover** hyperlinks at **run time!**
Representations contain information about **possible traversals**
The application navigates to the next resource depending on **link semantics**
Navigation **can be delegated** since interactions are **uniform** :-)

callout.text: Client-Server · Statelessness · Cacheability · Layered System · Code-on-Demand (Optional) · **Uniform Interface**

groups.heading: This “simple” mechanism renders the Web robust and flexible
points: This is why Web browsers **are general-purpose tools** and not hard-coded to specific applications!
This enables clients to **automatically adapt** when hyperlinks change! They don't even notice!

box.text: “HATEOAS” (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is a great way of creating highly flexible and interoperable systems beyond the Web! A lot more about this in Lecture 9 and Assignment 9.
